text:
**Education in Sweden** is structured around a comprehensive system starting with preschool (förskola) available to children aged 1 to 6, with free preschool education of at least three hours daily from age three. Compulsory education begins with a nine-year comprehensive school (grundskola) for children aged approximately 6–16, divided into lower, middle, and upper stages, covering 16 compulsory subjects including Swedish, mathematics, English, and science. From grade 6, students receive formal grades (A–F), and national tests are held in grades 3, 6, and 9 to ensure standardized assessment. After compulsory schooling, nearly all students attend elective upper secondary school (gymnasieskola) for three years, choosing among 18 national programmes divided into preparatory and vocational tracks, which qualify them for higher education or employment.
Higher education in Sweden follows the Bologna Process with bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees offered by universities and university colleges. Admission requires completion of upper secondary education and meeting language proficiency in Swedish and English. The Swedish Scholastic Aptitude Test (SweSAT) provides an alternative admissions route. Higher vocational education also exists, focusing on practical training but separate from the Bologna system. Since the 1990s, Sweden has allowed publicly funded independent (friskolor) primary and secondary schools, including for-profit and religious schools, though these have sparked debate regarding educational standards and inequality. Sweden’s education system experienced fluctuations in international assessment scores (PISA and PIRLS), with challenges attributed in part to immigrant student integration and testing issues. Student aid is provided through government loans and grants, and universities are required to support anti-discrimination policies.
